scenes.heading: A medicine had to survive its making.
scenes.narration: In medieval Cairo, pharmaceutical work did not end when the ingredients met. A syrup still had to withstand heat, storage, and the possibility of failure.
scenes.margin: An interpretative opening, not a reconstruction of an observed thirteenth-century pharmacy.

scenes.heading: A handbook cannot tell the whole story.
scenes.narration: The evidence comes from different places: a druggist's handbook, a hospital formulary, prescriptions preserved in the Genizah, and writings about market misconduct. Each answers a different question.
scenes.margin: Textual genres are not equivalent documentary evidence; preserve the distinction between instructions and observed shop transactions.

scenes.heading: Julāb was a material starting point.
scenes.narration: Al-Kūhīn described julep as the common base for sweet syrups, using the language of matter and form. The fruit gave the base a particular character.
scenes.arabic: أصل جميع الأشربة السكرية المتعارفة الجلاب
scenes.translation: The origin of the customary sweet syrups is julāb …
scenes.margin: Arabic excerpt typeset from quoted printed passage in the accepted manuscript; this is NOT a manuscript-page photograph.

scenes.heading: Heat. Clarify. Skim. Strain. Judge.
scenes.narration: The recipe moves through water and sugar, egg-white clarification, gentle heating, skimming, straining, and a carefully judged final consistency. These are practical instructions, not measured modern process controls.
scenes.margin: Schematic based on primary-text instructions; not footage of an actual medieval preparation.

scenes.heading: Crystallization required judgement.
scenes.narration: Al-Kūhīn even described syrup that had crystallized or deteriorated. A measured addition of hot water, renewed dissolution, and fruit water could restore an acceptable state.
scenes.translation: If the syrup crystallizes or becomes corrupted …
scenes.margin: Schematic of the stated repair instruction. Not a historical experiment, validated stability method or modern pharmaceutical reprocessing.

scenes.heading: Scarcity forced decisions.
scenes.narration: Substitution addressed unavailable or doubtful ingredients through perceived therapeutic action, dose, material character, and suitability. It was not modern chemical equivalence, and it was not permission for fraud.
scenes.margin: Conceptual decision diagram; no medieval ingredient approved as clinically bioequivalent.

scenes.eyebrow: A PRESCRIPTION IS NOT AN INVENTORY
scenes.heading: The page and the shelf could diverge.
scenes.narration: The Genizah prescription Or.1081 J39 joins an early electuary with a later decoction. It shows therapeutic instructions, but cannot prove every ingredient was available in the shop.
scenes.margin: Document identifier and reported sequence from scholarly analysis; no original Genizah photograph is reproduced without Cambridge permission.

scenes.heading: Reliability without modern standardization.
scenes.narration: This history is not an early version of Good Manufacturing Practice. It describes how materials, instructions, repair, and trust helped make medicines recognizable and usable before modern analytical testing.
scenes.margin: Modern concepts are used analytically; no historical genealogy to GMP claimed. Manuscript accepted 15 October 2026; not yet published.
